title: The relativistic electron
reading: In January 1928 — three months from now — Mr Dirac will publish a relativistic wave equation for the electron, first order in time and in space, using four-component wave functions. Spin and the electron's magnetic moment emerge automatically. But the equation also has solutions of negative energy. In 1931 he will propose that these correspond to a new particle of the same mass as the electron and opposite charge. In 1932 Carl Anderson in California will photograph such a particle in cosmic rays. It will be called the positron. Antimatter exists.
detail: Dirac's first interpretation (1929–30) filled the negative-energy states with a 'sea' and identified holes with protons; Weyl and Oppenheimer showed the holes must have the electron's mass, and Dirac predicted the anti-electron in 1931.

claim.label: The equation must be right
claim.summary: Dirac, shown his own future equation. He was documented as trusting mathematical beauty; that he hesitated for three years before predicting the positron is documented.
voice: If the equation gives spin without being asked to, it is probably right. The negative energies are a difficulty. I would not throw them away because they are inconvenient. I would expect them to mean something, even if I did not yet know what.
claim.reasoning: A correct equation's unexpected consequences should be taken seriously.

historical.note: Dirac first tried to identify the holes with protons (1929–30) before predicting the anti-electron in 1931. He later said his equation was more intelligent than its author.

claim.label: Brilliant and troubling
claim.summary: Heisenberg, writing to Pauli in 1928, was troubled by the negative-energy states of the Dirac equation.
voice: The spin coming out is marvellous. But negative energies mean an electron could fall forever, radiating. I do not see how that can be right. The theory is beautiful and physically unsound — both at once.

historical.note: Heisenberg complained to Pauli in 1928 about the negative-energy difficulty; his letters of the period call the situation one of the saddest chapters of modern physics.

claim.label: Sceptical of the sea
claim.summary: Pauli was sceptical of Dirac's hole theory and its infinite sea of negative-energy electrons.
voice: An infinite sea of electrons we cannot see, to explain a particle we have not found? Show me the particle.

historical.note: Pauli remained critical of hole theory even after the positron's discovery, and with Weisskopf (1934) gave a reformulation without the sea.

claim.label: Wait for the laboratory
claim.summary: Bohr was initially doubtful of the positron's reality.
voice: A new particle is a great deal to ask of an equation. I would wait for the cloud chamber.
